business_patterns.top_pattern: Mapping and classification gaps are inflating PPO Local spend
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: PPO Local spend in Not Mapped facility, DRG, and procedure buckets
business_patterns.pattern_details: A large share of the increase sits in unclassified facility, DRG, and procedure buckets, especially in GA, CA, and CT PPO Local claims. The same issue shows up in clinical findings through blank or unknown procedures and recurring Not Mapped classifications in outpatient misc, nursing facility, and outpatient surgery categories. This is a gating issue because it can distort both authorization targeting and provider action if the underlying classification is wrong.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Business actions on utilization, authorization, or contracting will be less reliable until these classification gaps are corrected.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Launch a joint data-quality and UM audit for Not Mapped facility, DRG, and procedure buckets in GA, CA, CT, ME, NY, and UNATTRIBUTED; correct mapping logic and re-run the affected authorization and provider reports before making policy changes.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Material spend is concentrated in Not Mapped and blank-value buckets across both operational and clinical findings, so classification must be verified before acting.
evidence_summary: GA Not Mapped facility claims added +$1.5M on 3,535 more claims, with only about +$105 higher paid per claim.
CA Not Mapped facility claims added +$1.2M on 2,922 more claims, with paid per claim nearly flat at about +$22.
CT Not Mapped facility claims added +$413K on 169 more claims.
Clinical validation buckets added about +$346K more across NF, OP Mgmt Oth Misc, and OP Surg with recurring Not Mapped, Null or Blank, or -3 values.

business_patterns.top_pattern: GA acute hospital spend is rising on both volume and unit cost
key_driver_codes: Other Circulatory System Diagnoses with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: GA acute hospital spend in PPO Local is increasing from a combination of more claims and higher paid amounts per claim. Most of the increase is concentrated in claims that are not well classified, which makes it harder to separate true utilization growth from reimbursement or care-pattern change. There are also smaller mapped signals in circulatory and cerebrovascular cases, so this is not only a single-code issue.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: GA is one of the largest identifiable acute hospital pressure points and needs coordinated UM, reimbursement, and data-quality action.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Perform a GA acute hospital drilldown by major hospital and claim type, validating the Not Mapped bucket first, then reviewing admission drivers, inpatient status, and reimbursement changes for the remaining mapped acute claims.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is overwhelmingly concentrated in Not Mapped acute hospital claims, so classification should be confirmed before broader provider or authorization changes.
evidence_summary: GA acute hospital spend added +$3.3M, almost all from the main Not Mapped acute bucket at +$3.26M.
The main GA acute bucket had 6,501 more claims and about +$225 higher paid per claim.
A smaller mapped circulatory signal added about +$13K with much higher paid per claim.
Additional GA cerebrovascular growth was volume-led, adding about +$18K on 4 more claims.

business_patterns.top_pattern: OH is the other major acute hospital pressure point, with smaller echoes in CO / PA / WI
key_driver_codes: Other Circulatory System Diagnoses with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: OH acute hospital spend in PPO Local shows the same combined volume and unit-cost pressure seen in GA, and it is the second-largest operational theme. Smaller similar increases also appear in CO / PA / WI acute hospitals, suggesting the issue is not fully isolated to one market. The provider-specific spikes are much smaller than the OH core trend, but they help identify where case-level review should start.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This is a large acute care cost trend with identifiable provider touchpoints that can support focused network and UM actions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Start with OH acute hospital claims to separate utilization growth from pricing changes, then run targeted case reviews for DEACONESS ILLINOIS MEDICAL CENTER and CONEMAUGH MEMORIAL MEDICAL CENTER to confirm whether the smaller provider spikes reflect contracting, coding, or case-severity differences.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The main OH increase is again concentrated in Not Mapped acute claims, so classification validation is required before scaling any intervention.
evidence_summary: OH acute hospital spend added +$2.6M, driven mainly by a Not Mapped bucket at +$2.57M.
The main OH acute bucket had 4,400 more claims and about +$132 higher paid per claim.
DEACONESS ILLINOIS MEDICAL CENTER added about +$61K on 2 claims, indicating a small but high-cost provider spike.
A smaller acute hospital pattern across CO / PA / WI added about +$80K, including +$24K at CONEMAUGH MEMORIAL MEDICAL CENTER.

business_patterns.top_pattern: GA outpatient specialty management is rising in renal care and chemotherapy-related services
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: GA outpatient specialty management / OP Mgmt Oth Misc
business_patterns.pattern_details: GA outpatient specialty management shows a focused clinical mix change rather than a broad outpatient trend. The growth is concentrated in renal management and chemotherapy-related services, with both more claims and higher paid amounts per claim. A provider-level signal at SOUTH AUGUSTA DIALYSIS CLINIC LLC supports a targeted review rather than a market-wide clinical policy change.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: This pattern points to a concentrated specialty-management opportunity for clinical review, provider engagement, and authorization refinement.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Route GA outpatient renal and chemotherapy-related claims for targeted clinical and UM review, starting with diagnosis-level pathways and the SOUTH AUGUSTA DIALYSIS CLINIC LLC provider signal to confirm whether referral mix, service intensity, or authorization rules need adjustment.
business_patterns.validation_reason: Recurring Not Mapped classification is present within the outpatient specialty findings, so the coding context should be confirmed alongside clinical review.
evidence_summary: GA OP Mgmt Oth Misc added +$1.6M overall.
Renal management with N186 and Medicine added +$912K on 216 more claims, with about +$1.8K higher paid per claim.
Chemotherapy-related services with Z5112 and Chemotherapy Drugs added +$648K on 37 more claims, with about +$6.4K higher paid per claim.
A related provider signal at SOUTH AUGUSTA DIALYSIS CLINIC LLC added about +$26K in the same outpatient management area.

business_patterns.top_pattern: GA non-acute site mix is adding cost across dialysis, SNF, rehab, and critical access
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: GA PPO Local non-acute facility spend
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Beyond GA acute hospitals, spend is also moving up across several non-acute settings, led by dialysis and followed by SNF, physical rehab, and critical access facilities. This looks like a provider and site-of-care economics issue, with higher use and higher paid amounts showing up across multiple facility types. The pattern is broad enough to justify a coordinated network and UM response rather than a single-provider intervention.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: If unmanaged, this broad non-acute mix shift can keep raising spend even if acute hospital trends improve.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Build a GA non-acute action plan that compares referral flow, authorization criteria, and reimbursement terms across dialysis, SNF, rehab, and critical access providers, starting with the largest dialysis and aftercare pathways.
evidence_summary: GA dialysis added +$917K on 216 more claims, with about +$1.7K higher paid per claim.
GA SNF added +$252K, mainly in musculoskeletal aftercare.
GA physical rehab added +$129K across musculoskeletal aftercare and cerebrovascular recovery cases.
GA critical access added +$116K, also concentrated in musculoskeletal aftercare.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Rare catastrophic IP Med/Surg cases are creating isolated but meaningful spikes
key_driver_codes: ECMO or Tracheostomy with Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours or Principal Diagnosis Except Face, Mouth and Neck with Major O.R. Procedures
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis with Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours
Major Small and Large Bowel Procedures with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: A small number of very high-cost IP Med/Surg cases account for a meaningful share of clinical spend increase. These are isolated catastrophic or near-catastrophic cases rather than a broad utilization trend, and several also carry blank or unknown procedure values. The right response is case-level validation and financial review, not broad utilization policy change.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A handful of severe inpatient cases can materially affect trend and should be validated for coding, severity, and financial handling.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Conduct case-level clinical and coding review for the identified high-cost IP Med/Surg admissions, including verification of severity, procedure coding, and any stop-loss or other high-cost claim handling.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is built from single-case events with blank or unknown procedure values, so case-level validation is essential before drawing broader conclusions.
evidence_summary: Rare IP Med/Surg cases added about +$510K from a small number of claims.
A CT ECMO or tracheostomy-related case added +$224K on a single claim.
A CO blood and blood-forming organs surgical case added +$46K on a single claim.
Provider-linked severe inpatient cases added about +$59K at DEACONESS ILLINOIS MEDICAL CENTER and +$21K at CONEMAUGH MEMORIAL MEDICAL CENTER.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CT mapped facilities show clear reimbursement pressure even without volume growth
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CT PPO Local / ACUTE HOSPITAL and HOME HEALTH - FREESTANDING
business_patterns.pattern_details: CT has a cleaner unit-cost story than the larger unmapped patterns. Spend is rising in mapped acute hospital and home health settings even though claim counts are down, which points more toward reimbursement pressure than utilization growth. This is a pricing and contract review issue first.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: CT appears to have real unit-cost inflation in mapped settings, making it a strong candidate for targeted reimbursement action.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a CT reimbursement review for acute hospital and home health claims to identify whether contract terms, payment edits, or case-rate changes are driving the higher paid amounts per claim.
evidence_summary: CT acute hospital added +$308K even with 6 fewer claims, with about +$2.3K higher paid per claim.
CT home health added +$71K even with 33 fewer claims, with about +$1.1K higher paid per claim.

business_patterns.top_pattern: SNF costs are rising outside GA through a mix of rate pressure and emerging volume
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
Other Circulatory System Diagnoses with CC
business_patterns.pattern_details: Outside GA, PPO Local SNF spend is increasing across several states, with different mixes of price and volume pressure. CA and NY are more clearly unit-cost-led, while PA and the smaller CA / OH pattern show a mix of added claims and higher paid amounts. This is a post-acute reimbursement and care-routing issue that should be handled separately from acute hospital work.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Post-acute cost pressure can persist after inpatient discharge and may require different network and UM levers than hospital trends.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review SNF reimbursement and discharge-routing practices in CA, PA, NY, and OH, prioritizing musculoskeletal aftercare and cerebrovascular recovery pathways where paid per claim is rising fastest.
evidence_summary: CA SNF added +$127K despite 12 fewer claims, with about +$860 higher paid per claim.
PA SNF added +$109K on 12 more claims, with about +$8.4K higher paid per claim.
NY SNF added +$29K with flat volume, with about +$7.2K higher paid per claim.
A smaller CA / OH SNF pattern added +$51K across circulatory and cerebrovascular recovery cases.

executive_summary.headline: The biggest PPO Local cost themes are large mapping and classification gaps, major acute hospital growth in GA and OH, and more targeted provider/site pressure in GA outpatient and post-acute settings.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: The clearest gating issue is the amount of spend sitting in Not Mapped and blank-value buckets, which affects both authorization targeting and provider action. After that, the main business levers are acute hospital mixed volume and unit-cost pressure in GA and OH, outpatient specialty growth in GA, and reimbursement pressure in CT and multi-state SNF settings.
recommended_focus_order: Fix mapping and classification gaps before changing authorization or provider strategy
Address GA and OH acute hospital mixed volume and unit-cost pressure
Target GA outpatient specialty, GA non-acute provider mix, CT reimbursement pressure, and multi-state SNF costs

notes: All 30 analytical groups were assigned to one of 8 business patterns.
A single consolidated validation pattern was used for material Not Mapped and blank-value issues across operational and clinical findings.
Smaller CO / PA / WI acute hospital findings were folded into the OH acute hospital story because the business lever is the same.
Rare IP Med/Surg outliers were kept separate because case-level actions differ from broad utilization or reimbursement actions.
